opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that language is a compression of the world, not the world itself. When humans write things down, we leave out an enormous amount because we assume the reader already shares a common physical and perceptual experience. Nobody writes "if I let go of this cup, it will fall to the floor and might shatter," because everyone already knows that. So a model trained mostly on text, even one that reasons at length in chains of thought, is reasoning over a representation that's missing much of the grounding we take for granted.

Scaling chains of thought helps a lot with things that are naturally expressed in language: math, code, logical deduction, planning in symbolic domains. There the reasoning really does live in the tokens. But much of understanding the world is spatial, temporal, and causal in ways that are awkward or lossy to put into words. Think about how an object deforms when you squeeze it, how a crowd moves, or how light changes across a room. You can describe these things verbally, but the description is a thin slice of the information. A model that only thinks in words is effectively trying to do physics through a keyhole.

There's also a data problem. We're approaching the limits of high-quality text on the internet, while video, audio, sensor data, and interaction data from the physical world are orders of magnitude richer and largely untapped. If you want models that can predict what happens next in the real world, act in it, and plan in it, you need them to learn from those modalities directly, not just from people's after-the-fact narration of them.

So I don't think language reasoning is a dead end. It's an incredibly powerful layer for abstraction and communication. But it has to sit on top of something that models the world more directly, whether you call it a world model or multimodal grounding. The next big jump will probably come from combining the two: models that can imagine and simulate in rich perceptual spaces, then use language to reason, explain, and coordinate on top of that.

r001.rationale: The response argues that text lacks perceptual grounding and that models need direct multimodal learning, but it does not cite failures to count objects in images.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd start by being careful about what "scaling chains of thought" has actually bought us. It's been enormous. Letting a model think longer in language before answering has unlocked math, coding, multi-step planning, things that looked out of reach three years ago. So I don't want to be dismissive of it. My skepticism is narrower: I don't think language-based reasoning, scaled further, gets you to a model that understands the world in the way we usually mean that phrase.

The core issue is that language is a lossy, human-authored compression of the world. When I write "the glass fell off the table," I'm leaving out almost everything. The trajectory, the sound, where the shards go, what it feels like to clean them up. A human reader fills that in from embodied experience. A model trained on text has to infer all of it from the statistical shadow that experience cast in writing. Chains of thought operate inside that same shadow. The model is reasoning in a medium that already discarded most of the information about physical reality. You can reason very carefully and still be reasoning about a sketch.

There's a second problem, which is that language only describes things people found worth describing. Nobody writes down that a cup stays on the table when you let go of it, or that your hand doesn't pass through the door. Those regularities are so obvious that they're nearly absent from text, yet they're the foundation of a world model. Video, interaction, sensorimotor data have the opposite property. They're dense with exactly the boring, ubiquitous structure that text omits. So if you want a model that knows how the world behaves rather than how people talk about it, I think you need learning signals that come from the world itself, not from descriptions of it.

The third thing is verification. Chains of thought work spectacularly in domains where the answer can be checked, like a proof or a unit test, because you can train the model to produce reasoning that leads to verifiable outcomes. Most of the world isn't like that. Predicting what happens when you push a box across a cluttered floor, or how a conversation will go, doesn't have a clean grader. Without one, longer reasoning tends to produce more fluent, more confident rationalizations rather than more accurate ones. I've seen plenty of cases where the model's reasoning reads beautifully and is simply wrong about the physical situation, and nothing in the training process would have caught that.

So where does that leave me? I think language will remain the interface and probably the medium for abstract reasoning, because it's the best tool humans ever built for that. But understanding requires grounding, and grounding comes from prediction over the raw stuff of the world, from acting and seeing what happens. The models that end up understanding the world will likely reason in language on top of representations that were learned from something richer than language. Scaling the reasoning layer alone is like making a very smart person read more books in a dark room. Useful, but at some point you have to turn on the lights.

r001.rationale: The response argues that text-based reasoning misses physical-world information, but it does not mention language models failing to count objects in images.

astra-6.text:
I think language is a powerful way to describe the world, but it’s only a partial description. There’s a lot that we learn through seeing things, interacting with them, and observing what happens. If you push an object, does it move? Does it fall? Those experiences give you information that isn’t necessarily captured in text.

Scaling chains of thought can help a model work through a problem, but that reasoning still needs to be grounded in something. A model can produce a long, coherent explanation while starting from an incorrect assumption. More reasoning doesn’t automatically give it the evidence needed to correct that assumption.

So I wouldn’t say language-based reasoning isn’t useful. It’s an important component. But to understand the world more deeply, models also need to learn from observation and action—to make predictions, see where those predictions fail, and update their understanding. The key is connecting reasoning to that feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says language is only a partial description and models need observation and action, but it does not cite language models’ failures to count objects in images as evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is a very powerful tool for reasoning, but it’s also a compressed description of the world. There’s a lot we know through seeing, hearing, moving, and interacting that never gets written down. So if you only scale reasoning over text, you’re asking the model to reconstruct all of that from descriptions that are necessarily incomplete.

For example, you can describe what happens when you push a cup toward the edge of a table. But understanding that situation also involves geometry, motion, friction, and the consequences of an action. A longer chain of thought doesn’t automatically give you a better model of those things. It can just produce a more elaborate explanation based on the same mistaken assumptions.

That doesn’t mean language-based reasoning isn’t useful. It’s extremely useful. But I think it needs to be grounded in perception and interaction, with some way to make predictions and check them against what actually happens. The important thing isn’t just whether a model can explain the world convincingly; it’s whether its understanding lets it predict and act reliably.

r001.rationale: The response argues that text-only reasoning lacks grounding in perception and interaction, but it does not mention language models failing to count objects in images as evidence.
